draft.title: Dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots
card: A dot plot puts one dot above a number line for each value. A tall pile of dots shows a value that occurs often.
A stem-and-leaf plot splits each value into a stem (the tens digit) and a leaf (the last digit). The leaves are put in order, and a note beside the plot explains how to read them.
Both displays keep every value, so you can read off the exact data. They also show clusters (where values bunch up) and gaps.
Example: in the stem-and-leaf plot above, the row 2 | 1 3 3 7 holds four scores, and they are 21, 23, 23 and 27.

1.alt: A dot plot of the number of pets in 10 homes. The values are 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 and 6. The tallest pile is at 2.

2.alt: A stem-and-leaf plot of 9 quiz scores: 12, 15, 21, 23, 23, 27, 34, 38 and 41. The note says 2 | 3 means 23.

draft.remember: Dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots keep every value and show clusters and gaps.

a.q: A stem-and-leaf plot has the note 3 | 0 means 30. What values are in the row 3 | 0 4 4 9?
a.why: The stem 3 is the tens digit and each leaf is a ones digit, so the row gives 30, 34, 34 and 39. Reading the leaves as 4, 4 and 9 alone ignores the stem.
a.clue: Join the stem to each leaf in turn.

b.q: The dot plot shows the number of goals scored by a netball team in 10 games. How many games had exactly 2 goals?
b.why: Count the dots above 2 on the number line. There are 4 dots there. The number 2 is the value, not the count of games.
b.clue: Count the dots, do not read the number.

fig.alt: A dot plot of goals in 10 games. The values are 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 and 5. There are 4 dots at 2.

problems.detail: Netball teams usually score dozens of goals a game, so 0 to 5 goals per game is unrealistic for Australian students who know the sport. Use a low-scoring sport such as soccer or hockey instead.
The figure's alt ends with 'There are 4 dots at 2', which states the answer outright for a student using a screen reader. The list of values is enough.
